primary_cause: COVID-driven hit to NBCUniversal ad film and park businesses. Universal Studios Hollywood soon forced to close
secondary_factors: General market panic. Reuters: U.S. ad industry could lose roughly $26B or 10.6% as live sports and consumer spending weakened. No major Comcast-specific negative announcement
store_description: Comcast's 3.0% decline looks most tied to NBCUniversal exposure rather than cable broadband. By March 11-12 investors were staring at potential park closures and a U.S. advertising pullback estimated at nearly $26B a bad setup for a company tied to film releases TV ads sports programming and physical attractions.

primary_cause: Semiconductor supply-chain and end-demand fears not a distinct AVGO event. Reuters reported Apple coronavirus warning dragging suppliers lower
secondary_factors: Broad tech selloff. ISM survey showed nearly 75% of U.S. companies seeing supply-chain disruptions. No fresh AVGO-specific negative headline
store_description: AVGO's 6.4% drop was most likely driven by investors repricing cyclical chip demand and supply exposure rather than a Broadcom-specific announcement. The market had fresh evidence of widespread supply-chain damage and had already punished hardware-linked names after Apple's coronavirus warning.

primary_cause: Oil-price war plus collapsing demand from COVID. Saudi-Russia blew up OPEC+ production pact. Brent -23.88% WTI -25.1% on Mar 9. COP pure upstream producer without refining offset especially exposed
secondary_factors: Equity-market panic and recession fears
store_description: COP's 6.7% decline was primarily an oil shock trade. Once Saudi and Russia shifted toward higher production into collapsing demand crude benchmarks crashed by roughly 24-25% in a day and investors sold E&P names directly levered to realized oil prices.

primary_cause: Bank-margin compression from rate collapse plus rising consumer credit-loss fears. 10-year briefly hit 0.318% on Mar 9. Reuters: financials hit because ultra-low rates squeeze bank profitability
secondary_factors: COF outsized credit-card exposure to travel and discretionary spending. No COF-specific corporate headline
store_description: COF's 8.8% drop was more than just banks down. The market was rapidly repricing two COF-specific risks at once: lower net interest income as Treasury yields cratered toward 0.318% and higher future charge-offs as COVID threatened card spending travel and household cash flow.

primary_cause: No material IBM-specific negative. Anticipated enterprise-spending slowdown and recession risk
secondary_factors: Broad tech selloff. Consulting and project deferrals. ISM: nearly 75% of companies reporting supply-chain disruption
store_description: IBM's 5.5% drop appears driven mainly by market repricing of enterprise IT and consulting budgets rather than a discrete IBM headline. As corporate America moved into contingency mode and supply-chain disruption spread investors started discounting delayed projects and weaker services demand.

primary_cause: Market looked through guidance reaffirmation and focused on aerospace and industrial exposure to collapsing travel and industrial demand. Honeywell reaffirmed Q1 and full-year guidance on Mar 10
secondary_factors: Broad cyclical industrial selloff and supply-chain risk
store_description: HON's drop was notable because the company had just reaffirmed guidance on March 10 which should have been supportive. Investors instead concluded that the guidance could quickly become stale as airline traffic weakened and aerospace-linked demand rolled over.

primary_cause: No HD-specific negative. Consumer-discretionary derating on recession fears
secondary_factors: Market-wide liquidation. Uncertainty over store traffic and discretionary projects
store_description: HD's 5.7% decline looks mostly like a cyclical consumer and recession trade not a company-event move. On March 11 investors were rapidly pricing in reduced household mobility weaker discretionary spending and a possible pause in larger home-improvement projects.

primary_cause: Bank and financial-sector repricing from collapsing rates and recession fears. 10-year below 1% on Mar 3 briefly 0.318% on Mar 9
secondary_factors: Threat to dealmaking underwriting and asset values from volatility shock. No major Goldman-specific headline
store_description: GS's 6.8% decline was less about credit losses and more about a broad hit to the financial complex: lower rates freezing risk appetite and the prospect that M&A capital markets activity and client balance-sheet risk could all deteriorate at once.

primary_cause: Fear of ad-spending weakness especially travel ads. Contemporaneous analyst estimate: Google travel-search ad revenue could fall ~$1B in Q1 and ~$3B in Q2
secondary_factors: Broad mega-cap tech selloff. Reuters: U.S. ad market faced possible $26B hit. Brand advertising weakened mid-March
store_description: GOOGL's 5.0% decline was likely tied to the sudden realization that Google's huge travel-ad funnel was at risk just as global mobility was shutting down. Estimates pointed to roughly $1B of lost travel-search ad spend in Q1 and $3B in Q2.

primary_cause: Expected auto-demand slowdown from COVID. Reuters Mar 11 reported analysts beginning to forecast U.S. auto-sales slowdown
secondary_factors: Supply-chain worries. GM and peers said production not yet disrupted in U.S. Stock sold on forward demand fears before full plant shutdowns
store_description: GM's 4.1% decline appears driven by deteriorating auto-demand expectations rather than an immediate factory halt. Reuters said on March 11 that analysts were starting to model weaker showroom traffic and sales even though Detroit automakers still said U.S. production had not yet been disrupted.

primary_cause: GE Aviation exposure to airline collapse. Major exposure to aviation and industrial cyclicality. Reuters later described GE aviation hit particularly hard by coronavirus recession
secondary_factors: Leverage and turnaround concerns. Industrial recession risk. No fresh GE-specific headline
store_description: GE's 7.2% decline was likely driven by the market zeroing in on GE Aviation one of the company's most important profit engines just as airline demand began to crater. With passenger traffic falling and the travel outlook worsening investors had a direct line from COVID to weaker engine deliveries services revenue and cash flow.

primary_cause: Gulfstream and business-aviation exposure to travel shock. Business-jet exposure through Gulfstream vulnerable to sudden stop in travel and corporate spending
secondary_factors: Broad industrial and defense selloff. Reuters later showed pandemic disruption hit GD aerospace materially. No distinct GD corporate event
store_description: GD's 4.4% drop likely reflected investor concern over Gulfstream first and defense second. Defense revenue is usually steadier but Gulfstream is highly sensitive to corporate travel and capital-spending confidence both of which deteriorated sharply as Europe travel restrictions were announced.

primary_cause: Travel-ad and broader ad-market weakness. Same setup as GOOGL. ~$1B less travel-search ad spend Q1 ~$3B less Q2
secondary_factors: Mega-cap tech de-risking. Broader U.S. ad-market hit ~$26B. No class-share-specific item
store_description: GOOG fell for the same reason GOOGL did: investors were rapidly discounting lower ad demand especially in travel one of Google's most important advertiser verticals. Estimates circulating at the time called for about $1B less travel-search ad spend in Q1 and $3B less in Q2.

primary_cause: Air-freight and global-commerce shock from COVID and travel restrictions. Reduced passenger flying constrains global air-cargo capacity. Cross-border commerce under pressure
secondary_factors: Broad cyclical selloff and recession fears. No FedEx-specific negative in prior 3 days
store_description: FDX's 8.0% decline likely reflected the market pricing a severe logistics shock. As passenger flights were being cut and Europe travel restrictions hit investors could see both sides of the problem for FedEx: weaker premium and global shipment demand and disrupted air network economics.

primary_cause: Industrial and energy capex fears. Meaningful exposure to industrial capex and energy end markets. Crude down ~24-25% in a day
secondary_factors: General market liquidation and supply-chain disruption. No Emerson-specific headline
store_description: EMR's 3.2% drop appears mainly tied to its cyclical industrial mix rather than a discrete company event. With crude down about 24-25% in a day and recession odds spiking the market was cutting expectations for process automation energy projects and broader industrial spending.

primary_cause: No material Duke-specific headline. Market-wide deleveraging and liquidity selling. Utilities normally defensive but forced-risk-off
secondary_factors: Economic uncertainty around commercial and industrial load demand
store_description: DUK's 4.3% fall is harder to tie to a company-specific news item. Utilities are normally defensive which suggests the move was driven more by indiscriminate selling and concerns about a broad economic freeze hitting commercial and industrial power demand.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC context. Reuters reported Disney would close California and Florida parks and Disneyland Paris from that weekend. Imminent theme-park film and travel disruption from COVID
secondary_factors: Travel restrictions. Sports and media disruption. Even before formal Mar 12 release market already discounting park closures
store_description: Disney was one of the clearest COVID-exposure stories. Reuters reported Disney would close its California and Florida parks and Disneyland Paris from that weekend. Even before the formal release on March 12 the market was already discounting that risk as gathering restrictions intensified.

primary_cause: No negative DHR-specific headline. Broad market risk-off before COVID-test upside recognized. Cepheid rapid-test EUA only arrived Mar 21-22 after this drop
secondary_factors: Near-term concern about hospital and lab purchasing disruption and recession
store_description: DHR's 3.4% decline does not appear caused by adverse company news. More likely investors sold it with the broader market before Danaher's diagnostic upside became visible. Cepheid's rapid SARS-CoV-2 test authorization did not arrive until roughly ten days later.

primary_cause: Industrial-demand and manufacturing-disruption fears. Reuters later reported Deere faced supply-chain-related production suspensions
secondary_factors: Recession risk. Supply-chain concerns. Nearly 75% of surveyed companies reporting supply-chain disruption. No Deere-specific headline in Mar 8-11
store_description: DE's 5.9% decline seems driven by investors marking down capital-equipment demand and supply continuity not by a discrete Deere announcement. With nearly 75% of surveyed U.S. companies reporting supply-chain disruption heavy-equipment manufacturers were easy targets for de-risking.

primary_cause: Enterprise IT spending slowdown plus supply-chain disruption fears. China-linked supply exposure. ISM: almost 75% of firms facing supply-chain problems
secondary_factors: Broad tech correction and recession risk. No Cisco-specific negative update
store_description: CSCO's 7.6% fall likely reflected a harsh repricing of hardware and enterprise-budget risk rather than a fresh Cisco headline. By March 11 investors had evidence that most U.S. companies were already seeing supply-chain problems and they were extrapolating that into weaker orders and delayed deployments.
